questions.question: Consider the diagram, which shows the structure $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_n\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ with a non-polar hydrocarbon tail and a polar head. What structure does this diagram represent?
questions.answer: The structure is the sodium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid ($-\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ head on a hydrocarbon tail), which is a soap (A). An anionic detergent has a sulfonate/sulfate head, and a cationic detergent has a positively charged (e.g. ammonium) head.

questions.question: What is the conjugate base of $\text{HSO}_4^-$?
questions.answer: A conjugate base is formed when the acid donates a proton: $\text{HSO}_4^- \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{SO}_4^{2-}$, so the conjugate base is $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ (D).

questions.question: Which option is the correct equation for the incomplete combustion of ethanol?
questions.answer: Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide and water. Option C is balanced (O: $1 + 4 = 2 + 3$). D is complete combustion; A and B produce hydrogen gas, which is not a combustion product.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about activation energy, $E_a$, and equilibrium is correct?
options: Lowering the $E_a$ will cause a reaction to reach equilibrium faster.
Lowering the $E_a$ will shift the position of equilibrium to increase product yield.
$E_a$ does not apply to equilibrium reactions.
questions.answer: Lowering $E_a$ (e.g. with a catalyst) increases the rates of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position (and yield) is unchanged (A).

questions.question: Consider the titration curve shown. Based on the curve, what can be concluded about the titration?
options: A strong acid was added to a strong base.
A strong acid was added to a weak base.
A strong base was added to a weak acid.
A weak acid was added to a weak base.
questions.answer: The pH starts high (about 11) and decreases, so acid is being added to a base. The initial pH is only about 11 with a buffer region near pH 9, typical of a weak base, and the pH falls to about 1 after equivalence, showing a strong acid titrant. The equivalence point is below 7. So a strong acid was added to a weak base (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows molecules $P$ ($\text{HCOOH}$) and $Q$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$) reacting to form molecule $R$ ($\text{HCONHCH}_3$) and water. Which row identifies the molecule types?
options: P: alcohol; Q: amine; R: ester
P: carboxylic acid; Q: amide; R: amine
P: carboxylic acid; Q: amine; R: amide
P: aldehyde; Q: amide; R: ketone
questions.answer: $P$ contains $-\text{COOH}$ (methanoic acid, a carboxylic acid), $Q$ contains $-\text{NH}_2$ (methanamine, an amine), and $R$ contains $-\text{CONH}-$ (N-methylmethanamide, an amide) (C).

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the molecule shown?
questions.answer: The longest chain has 4 carbons (butane) with Cl and F on C2 and C3. Either numbering gives locants 2,3, and substituents are listed alphabetically (chloro before fluoro): 2-chloro-3-fluorobutane (A).

questions.question: How many isomers does the formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2$ have?
questions.answer: The two bromine atoms can be on the same carbon (1,1-dibromoethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBr}_2$) or on different carbons (1,2-dibromoethane, $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCH}_2\text{Br}$), so there are 2 isomers (B).

questions.question: 100 mL of 0.4 M nitric acid, $\text{HNO}_3$, is added to 100 mL of 0.1 M barium hydroxide, $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$. What is the pH of the resulting solution?
What mass of silver chloride ($MM = 143.4$) will dissolve in 1.00 L of water? The $K_{sp}$ of AgCl is $1.8 \times 10^{-10}$.

A student drew a diagram that illustrated the flow of matter and energy in closed and open systems. They used the key shown (solid arrow = exchange of matter with the surroundings; dashed arrow = exchange of energy with the surroundings). Which of the following could be the student's diagram?
questions.answer: A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings (dashed arrows only); an open system exchanges both matter and energy (solid and dashed arrows in and out). Only C shows this.

questions.question:
The production of hydrogen occurs by the reaction of methane with steam. The reaction mixture reaches a state of dynamic equilibrium.

$$\text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \qquad \Delta H = +206\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which of the following shows how the equilibrium yield of hydrogen and the value of the equilibrium constant are affected by the changes shown?

| | Change | Effect on equilibrium yield of $\text{H}_2(g)$ | Effect on value of $K_{eq}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Increase pressure | decrease | decrease |
| B | Add a catalyst | increase | no effect |
| C | Increase temperature | increase | increase |
| D | Remove CO(g) as formed | increase | increase |
questions.answer: The forward reaction is endothermic, so increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium right, increasing the yield of $\text{H}_2$ and increasing $K_{eq}$ (C). Pressure and concentration changes do not change $K_{eq}$ (only temperature does), and a catalyst changes neither yield nor $K_{eq}$.

questions.question: A simplified mass spectrum of butanoic acid is shown. What does the peak with the mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, of 73 represent?
questions.answer: Butanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, has $M = 88$. The peak at 73 is $88 - 15$, i.e. loss of a $\text{CH}_3$ group, leaving the positively charged fragment $[\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}]^+$ (D). Mass spectrometry detects only positive ions, and the greatest m/z peak is not 73 (there are small peaks above it; the molecular ion would be at 88).

questions.question: The structure of 2,2-dimethylbutane ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$) is shown. In a particular chlorination reaction, a single hydrogen atom of 2,2-dimethylbutane is replaced by one chlorine atom. More than one compound with the formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{Cl}$ can be formed. How many different compounds could be formed in this monosubstitution reaction?
questions.answer: 2,2-dimethylbutane has three different hydrogen environments: the nine equivalent H on the three $\text{CH}_3$ groups attached to C2, the H on the $\text{CH}_2$ (C3), and the H on the terminal $\text{CH}_3$ (C4). Substituting each gives a different product, so 3 compounds (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows two reactions of substance X: with HBr it forms Y, and with $\text{H}_2$/Pd catalyst it forms $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$. Determine the molecular formulae of substances X and Y.
questions.answer: X undergoes addition with $\text{H}_2$ to form the alkane $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$, so X is the alkene $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ (one $\text{H}_2$ added). Addition of HBr across the double bond gives $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}\text{Br}$ (B).

questions.question:
Iron(III) forms a variety of coloured complex ions. One such example is that produced by the reaction with salicylic acid ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$):

$$\underset{\text{pale yellow}}{\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)} + \text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \underset{\text{violet}}{\text{Fe(C}_7\text{H}_5\text{O}_3)^{2+}(aq)} + \text{H}^+(aq)$$

Which of the following will decrease the yield of the violet complex, $\text{Fe(C}_7\text{H}_5\text{O}_3)^{2+}$?
options: Lowering the pH of the solution
Raising the pH of the solution
questions.answer: Lowering the pH increases $[\text{H}^+]$, a product, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts left and the yield of the violet complex decreases (A). Raising the pH or adding $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ shifts it right; adding more solid does not change the position.

questions.question: Which of the following combinations of solutions will form the most effective buffer solution?
options: 20 mL of 0.3 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and 10 mL of 0.2 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{NaCH}_3\text{COO}$
10 mL of 0.3 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and 20 mL of 0.2 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$
20 mL of 0.3 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH and 10 mL of 0.3 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{NaCH}_3\text{COO}$
20 mL of 0.3 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ and 20 mL of 0.3 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{NaHCO}_3$
questions.answer: A buffer is a weak acid and its conjugate base; it is most effective when they are present in equal (and reasonably large) amounts. D has equal amounts (6 mmol each) of $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ and $\text{HCO}_3^-$. A is a buffer but with an uneven ratio (6 mmol acid : 2 mmol base); B and C are not buffers.

questions.question: The graph shows the absorption spectra of three food dyes: Blue No. 1, Red No. 2 and Yellow No. 4. Which one of the following is the best wavelength to determine the concentration of Red No. 2 dye in a solution containing a mixture of all three dyes?
questions.answer: The wavelength chosen must be absorbed by Red No. 2 but not by the other dyes. At 500 nm Red No. 2 absorbs (about 0.3) while Yellow No. 4 and Blue No. 1 both have zero absorbance (B). At 540 nm Red No. 2 is at its maximum, but Blue No. 1 also absorbs significantly, causing interference.

questions.question:
The equation shows the reaction of HF with water.

$$\text{HF}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \text{F}^-(aq)$$

A 0.13 M solution of HF has a pH of 2.05. What is the p$K_b$ of $\text{F}^-$?

Temperature can affect the value of the equilibrium constant for the ionisation of water ($K_w$). The graph shows values for p$K_w$ for temperatures between 0 °C and 100 °C. A student placed solutions in a water bath at 60 °C to determine if temperature affected the resulting pH of the following reaction. 10.0 mL of 0.15 mol L$^{-1}$ KOH was added to 5 mL of distilled water. Predict the final pH of the solution at 60 °C.

Molecules of propan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$) and propanone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$) each contain three carbon atoms. Name the shape around the central C atom in a molecule of each compound.
questions.answer:
- Propan-2-ol: **tetrahedral** (the central carbon has four single bonds: two C, one O, one H).
- Propanone: **trigonal planar** (the central carbon has a C=O double bond and two C–C single bonds, i.e. three electron domains).

questions.question: Explain why propanone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$) has a lower boiling point than propan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$).
questions.answer: Boiling requires overcoming the intermolecular forces between molecules. Both molecules have similar molar masses and therefore similar dispersion forces. Propanone has a polar carbonyl group (C=O), so its strongest intermolecular forces are dipole–dipole forces; it has no H atom bonded to O, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself. Propan-2-ol has a hydroxyl group (O–H), so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other. Hydrogen bonds are stronger than dipole–dipole forces, so less energy is needed to separate propanone molecules and propanone has the lower boiling point.

questions.question: Consider the equilibrium reaction $2\text{NOCl}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$. Predict which reaction (forward or reverse) favours maximum entropy. Explain your answer.
questions.answer: The **forward** reaction favours maximum entropy. The products side has 3 moles of gas compared with 2 moles of gas on the reactant side; more gas particles means more disorder (more possible arrangements), so the forward reaction increases entropy ($\Delta S > 0$).

questions.question: Consider the equilibrium reaction $2\text{NOCl}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$, for which the forward reaction increases entropy (3 mol of gas produced from 2 mol). Predict whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
questions.answer: The forward reaction is **endothermic**. For a reaction to reach equilibrium (rather than going to completion), the entropy and enthalpy drives must oppose each other: at equilibrium $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0$. Since the forward reaction has $\Delta S > 0$ (favoured by entropy), for $\Delta G$ to be able to equal zero $\Delta H$ must also be positive. So the forward reaction is favoured by entropy, the reverse reaction is favoured by enthalpy (minimum energy), and the forward reaction is endothermic.

questions.question: Consider the equilibrium reaction $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$. A 2.0 L container is filled with 0.070 mol of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$. Equilibrium is reached after 20.0 minutes, at which time there is 0.040 mol $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ and 0.060 mol of $\text{NO}_2$. Sketch and label a graph of the concentrations of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ and $\text{NO}_2$ (concentration in mol L$^{-1}$, 0 to 0.080, against time, 0 to 50 min) for the time period 0 to 30.0 minutes.
questions.answer:
Concentrations (divide moles by 2.0 L):
- $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]$ starts at $0.070/2.0 = 0.035$ mol L$^{-1}$ and decreases along a curve (steep at first, then levelling off) to $0.040/2.0 = 0.020$ mol L$^{-1}$ at 20.0 min.
- $[\text{NO}_2]$ starts at 0 and increases along a curve to $0.060/2.0 = 0.030$ mol L$^{-1}$ at 20.0 min. (It rises twice as much as $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]$ falls, by the 1 : 2 ratio.)
- From 20.0 to 30.0 min both lines are horizontal (constant concentrations at equilibrium).

See the graph (0–30 min section).

questions.question: Consider the equilibrium reaction $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$ in a 2.0 L container. At equilibrium, $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4] = 0.020$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{NO}_2] = 0.030$ mol L$^{-1}$. At time 30.0 minutes a malfunction with the equipment causes the volume to double and the equilibrium is disturbed. Equilibrium is reached again after 10 minutes. Sketch and label a graph of the concentrations of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ and $\text{NO}_2$ for the time period 30.0 to 50.0 minutes.
questions.answer:
- At 30.0 min the volume doubles, so both concentrations instantly halve (vertical drops): $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]$ 0.020 → 0.010 and $[\text{NO}_2]$ 0.030 → 0.015 mol L$^{-1}$.
- The lower pressure favours the side with more moles of gas (Le Chatelier), so the equilibrium shifts right: $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]$ decreases and $[\text{NO}_2]$ increases, with the rise in $[\text{NO}_2]$ twice the fall in $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]$. Neither returns to its original level.
- Quantitatively, $K = 0.030^2/0.020 = 0.045$. Solving $\dfrac{(0.015+2x)^2}{0.010-x} = 0.045$ gives $x \approx 0.0020$, so the new equilibrium (reached at 40.0 min, then horizontal to 50.0 min) is $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4] \approx 0.0080$ and $[\text{NO}_2] \approx 0.019$ mol L$^{-1}$.

See the graph (30–50 min section).

*Note: the school's sample graph shows $[\text{NO}_2]$ rising to about 0.025 and $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]$ falling to about 0.005 mol L$^{-1}$, which is not consistent with $K = 0.045$; the values above are.*

questions.question: Propan-1-ol can react with methanoic acid to produce an organic molecule. The diagram shows the apparatus used for this reaction (reflux). Identify the type of reaction.
questions.answer: Esterification (a condensation reaction).

questions.question: Propan-1-ol reacts with methanoic acid (heated under reflux with a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst) to produce an organic molecule. Write a balanced structural chemical equation for the reaction.
questions.answer:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{HCOOH} \;\overset{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ \text{heat}}{\rightleftharpoons}\; \text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

propan-1-ol + methanoic acid ⇌ propyl methanoate + water. In the structural formulae, the O–H of the alcohol and the C(=O)–OH of the acid are drawn in full; the product is H–C(=O)–O–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–CH$_3$ (ester link –COO–). An equilibrium arrow must be used and water must be included.

questions.question: Propan-1-ol and methanoic acid are heated under reflux in a round-bottom flask to produce an ester. Identify an appropriate source of heat. Justify your answer.
questions.answer: A hot plate or heating mantle (an electric heat source with no naked flame). The alcohol, the acid and the ester product are volatile and flammable, so using a Bunsen burner could ignite the vapours and cause a fire or explosion; an electric heater avoids an open flame.

questions.question: You have performed the esterification of propan-1-ol with methanoic acid in your study of Chemistry. Explain two steps you used to purify your product in the science laboratory. Refer to reagents and equipment used.
questions.answer:
Any two of:
1. **Washing with water in a separating funnel:** the reaction mixture is shaken with water in a separating funnel. The unreacted alcohol, acid and sulfuric acid catalyst are soluble in water, while the ester is insoluble and forms a separate layer, so the aqueous layer is run off and discarded.
2. **Washing with sodium carbonate (or sodium hydrogen carbonate) solution in a separating funnel:** this neutralises and removes any remaining sulfuric acid and methanoic acid (forming soluble salts and $\text{CO}_2$); the aqueous layer is again run off.
3. **Drying:** adding anhydrous calcium chloride (or another drying agent such as anhydrous magnesium sulfate) to the ester layer to remove traces of water, then filtering/decanting.
4. **Distillation:** distilling the mixture and collecting the fraction at the ester's boiling point, separating the ester from remaining water and alcohol.

questions.question:
A student was given 4 colourless liquids labelled A, B, C and D. They were known to be ethanol, ethanoic acid, pentane and hex-3-ene, but the exact identity of each liquid was unknown. The student tested the properties of each liquid and obtained the following results.

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility in water | insoluble | soluble | soluble | insoluble |
| Addition of red-coloured bromine solution $(aq)$ (absence of UV light) | colour disappears | no immediate reaction | no immediate reaction | no immediate reaction |
| Addition of sodium carbonate solution $(aq)$ | no reaction | gas evolved | no reaction | no reaction |

Identify each of the liquids.
questions.answer:
- A = hex-3-ene (insoluble and decolourises bromine water: C=C double bond)
- B = ethanoic acid (soluble and produces $\text{CO}_2$ gas with sodium carbonate)
- C = ethanol (soluble but not acidic)
- D = pentane (insoluble and does not react with bromine water without UV light)

questions.question: Liquid A is hex-3-ene, which decolourises red-brown bromine water. Identify the type of reaction occurring between hex-3-ene and bromine solution **and** write a balanced structural equation.
questions.answer:
**Addition reaction** (the bromine adds across the C=C double bond).

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}{=}\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

hex-3-ene + bromine → 3,4-dibromohexane (drawn with all bonds shown in a structural equation).

questions.question: Four liquids are ethanol, ethanoic acid, pentane and hex-3-ene. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are soluble in water; pentane and hex-3-ene are insoluble. Discuss the different solubilities of the 4 compounds in water.
questions.answer:
- **Pentane and hex-3-ene** are hydrocarbons, which are non-polar. Their only intermolecular forces are weak dispersion forces, and they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. The attractions between hydrocarbon and water molecules are too weak to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules, so they are insoluble.
- **Ethanol** is polar and contains a hydroxyl (–OH) group, so it forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules; its hydrocarbon chain is short, so it is soluble (miscible).
- **Ethanoic acid** is polar and its carboxyl group (–COOH, with C=O and O–H) forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules; it also partially ionises in water. Its short chain means it is soluble.

questions.question:
A student was investigating the properties of acids and constructed the following table. Complete the missing entries for hydrochloric acid (its type of acid and pH at 25 °C).

| Acid | Concentration (mol L$^{-1}$) | Type of acid | Available protons | pH at 25 °C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hydrocyanic acid (HCN) | 0.50 | weak | monoprotic | 4.72 |
| Hydrochloric acid (HCl) | 0.50 | ? | monoprotic | ? |
questions.answer: HCl is a **strong** acid, so it ionises completely: $[\text{H}^+] = 0.50$ M and pH $= -\log(0.50) = 0.30$.

questions.question: A 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrocyanic acid (HCN, a weak monoprotic acid) has a pH of 4.72 at 25 °C. Calculate the $K_a$ of hydrocyanic acid.
questions.answer:
$\text{HCN}(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{CN}^-(aq)$, $\quad K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{CN}^-]}{[\text{HCN}]}$

$[\text{H}^+] = [\text{CN}^-] = 10^{-4.72} = 1.91\times10^{-5}$ M.

At equilibrium $[\text{HCN}] = 0.50 - 1.91\times10^{-5} \approx 0.50$ M (the amount ionised is negligible, much less than 5%, because HCN is a weak acid).

$$K_a = \frac{(10^{-4.72})^2}{0.50} = \frac{3.63\times10^{-10}}{0.50} = 7.3\times10^{-10}$$

questions.question: A buffer solution is prepared by combining 100 mL of 0.010 M hypochlorous acid (HClO) and 0.107 g of solid NaClO. $K_a(\text{HClO}) = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}$. Calculate the pH of this buffer solution and explain the classification of the solution as a buffer using appropriate equation/s in your answer.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{NaClO}) = \dfrac{0.107}{22.99 + 35.45 + 16.00} = \dfrac{0.107}{74.44} = 1.437\times10^{-3}$ mol, so $[\text{ClO}^-] = \dfrac{1.437\times10^{-3}}{0.100} = 0.01437$ M; $[\text{HClO}] = 0.010$ M.

$$K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{ClO}^-]}{[\text{HClO}]} \Rightarrow [\text{H}^+] = \frac{3.0\times10^{-8}\times0.010}{0.01437} = 2.09\times10^{-8}\ \text{M}$$

pH $= -\log(2.09\times10^{-8}) = 7.68$

The solution is a buffer because it contains significant amounts of a weak acid (HClO) and its conjugate base ($\text{ClO}^-$) in equilibrium: $\text{HClO}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \text{ClO}^-(aq)$. If a small amount of acid is added, $\text{ClO}^-$ reacts with it ($\text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ \rightarrow \text{HClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$); if a small amount of base is added, HClO neutralises it ($\text{HClO} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$). The equilibrium shifts to counteract the change, so the pH stays nearly constant.

questions.question: The diagram shows the major components of a colourimeter. The concentration of phosphate in a water sample can be determined using a colourimeter. Phosphate is colourless; it can be reacted with ammonium molybdate and ascorbic acid in the presence of sulfuric acid to form a blue complex. An analytical chemist used the colour wheel shown to select a suitable filter to determine the phosphate concentration of an industrial effluent water sample. Identify the most appropriate colour for the filter in the colourimeter for this analysis.
questions.answer: **Yellow.** The blue complex absorbs most strongly the complementary colour, which is directly opposite blue on the colour wheel (yellow), so a yellow filter gives the greatest sensitivity.

questions.question:
Solutions of known phosphate concentration were used to calibrate a colourimeter, giving the absorbance values in the table. Draw a labelled graph of the data (calibration curve) with a straight line of best fit.

| Concentration (mg/L) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| 0.00 | 0.003 |
| 0.15 | 0.095 |
| 0.30 | 0.194 |
| 0.45 | 0.290 |
| 0.60 | 0.378 |
| 0.90 | 0.573 |
| 1.20 | 0.745 |
questions.answer: Plot concentration (mg L$^{-1}$) on the horizontal axis (independent variable) and absorbance on the vertical axis, with even scales (e.g. 0–1.4 mg L$^{-1}$ and 0–0.8), a title and labelled axes with units. Plot each point accurately and draw a single straight line of best fit with a ruler passing through (or very close to) the origin; the gradient is about 0.62 absorbance units per mg L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: A colourimeter was calibrated with phosphate standards; the line of best fit is approximately Absorbance $= 0.622 \times$ concentration (mg L$^{-1}$) $+ 0.005$ (absorbance 0.003 at 0.00 mg/L, 0.378 at 0.60 mg/L and 0.745 at 1.20 mg/L). The Environment Protection Authority (EPA) recommends that effluent from industrial sites entering a waterway should have a limit of $5.0 \times 10^{-7}$ mol L$^{-1}$ of phosphate to avoid algae growth. 10 mL of a filtered effluent sample was placed in a 100 mL volumetric flask and made up to the mark with distilled water. This sample was tested using the colourimeter. The absorbance value for this solution was 0.4440. Use the graphed data to determine the concentration of phosphate in the effluent and determine if the effluent water complies with EPA recommendations.
questions.answer:
From the calibration graph, absorbance 0.444 corresponds to about **0.70 mg L$^{-1}$** in the diluted sample.

The sample was diluted 10 times (10 mL to 100 mL), so the effluent contains $0.70 \times 10 = 7.0$ mg L$^{-1}$ $= 7.0\times10^{-3}$ g L$^{-1}$ of phosphate.

$M(\text{PO}_4^{3-}) = 30.97 + 4(16.00) = 94.97$ g mol$^{-1}$

$[\text{PO}_4^{3-}] = \dfrac{7.0\times10^{-3}}{94.97} = 7.4\times10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$

This is much greater than the EPA limit of $5.0\times10^{-7}$ mol L$^{-1}$, so the effluent does **not** comply.

questions.question: As a precaution, phosphate can be reduced in effluent wastewater before it enters waterways using precipitation. In the research laboratory, 100 mL of the wastewater containing $2.1 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ of phosphate ions is tested. Will a precipitate of calcium phosphate form when the wastewater sample is added to 200 mL of $5 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$ calcium chloride? ($K_{sp}$ of $\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2 = 2.07\times10^{-33}$.) Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
$\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2(s) \rightleftharpoons 3\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{PO}_4^{3-}(aq)$, $\quad K_{sp} = [\text{Ca}^{2+}]^3[\text{PO}_4^{3-}]^2$

$n(\text{PO}_4^{3-}) = 2.1\times10^{-4}\times0.100 = 2.1\times10^{-5}$ mol; $n(\text{Ca}^{2+}) = 5\times10^{-2}\times0.200 = 1.0\times10^{-2}$ mol.

Total volume $= 300$ mL $= 0.300$ L:
$[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = 0.0100/0.300 = 0.0333$ M; $[\text{PO}_4^{3-}] = 2.1\times10^{-5}/0.300 = 7.0\times10^{-5}$ M.

$$Q = (0.0333)^3(7.0\times10^{-5})^2 = (3.70\times10^{-5})(4.9\times10^{-9}) = 1.8\times10^{-13}$$

Since $Q = 1.8\times10^{-13} > K_{sp} = 2.07\times10^{-33}$, a precipitate of calcium phosphate **will form**.

*Note: the school's guidelines quote $K_{sp} = 2.07\times10^{-29}$; the data-sheet value is $2.07\times10^{-33}$. The conclusion is the same.*

questions.question: Two different compounds A and B are isomers with the molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$. They undergo a series of reactions as shown in the flow chart: A is oxidised by acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ to C ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$); B is oxidised by acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ to D, which shows no reaction with further acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$; C reacts with $\text{NH}_3$ to form E. Draw (or give the full structural formula of) each compound, A to E.
questions.answer:
- **A: propan-1-ol**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (a primary alcohol, oxidised to a carboxylic acid).
- **B: propan-2-ol**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ (a secondary alcohol, oxidised to a ketone).
- **C: propanoic acid**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$).
- **D: propanone**, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ (a ketone, which cannot be oxidised further, so no reaction with $\text{KMnO}_4$).
- **E: ammonium propanoate**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-\ \text{NH}_4^+$, formed by the acid–base reaction of propanoic acid with ammonia. (If heated, the ammonium salt dehydrates to propanamide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$, which was also accepted.)

All structures should be drawn with every bond shown, including the O–H bonds.

questions.question: Consider the equilibrium reaction $\text{O}_2(g) + 2\text{SO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $\Delta H = -197$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. 2.0 moles of oxygen was heated with 0.89 moles of sulfur dioxide in a 2.0 L sealed container at 25 °C. When equilibrium was established, 0.80 moles of sulfur trioxide was present. Calculate $K_{eq}$ at 25 °C.

Consider the equilibrium reaction $\text{O}_2(g) + 2\text{SO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $\Delta H = -197$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. In the industrial process used to produce sulfur trioxide, the conditions shown in the flow chart are used: reactants sulfur dioxide and oxygen in a 1 : 1 ratio by volume; temperature 400–450 °C; pressure 200 kPa; $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ catalyst. Analyse the conditions chosen by engineers for this chemical synthesis process.
questions.answer:
In industrial synthesis the aim is to obtain a high yield at a fast rate, without compromising cost and safety.

- **Temperature (400–450 °C):** the forward reaction is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle a low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield of $\text{SO}_3$. However, at low temperature the rate is too slow because few collisions have energy greater than $E_a$. A moderately high temperature is a **compromise** between an acceptable yield and a fast rate.
- **Pressure (200 kPa):** there are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium right and increases the yield and rate. Very high pressures are costly and dangerous (expensive equipment, energy), so a moderate pressure is a compromise between yield and cost/safety (the yield is already high).
- **Ratio 1 : 1 by volume:** the stoichiometric ratio is 1 $\text{O}_2$ : 2 $\text{SO}_2$, so oxygen is in excess. Increasing $[\text{O}_2]$ shifts the equilibrium right, increasing conversion of the toxic, more expensive $\text{SO}_2$; oxygen (from air) is cheap and safe.
- **$\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ catalyst:** lowers the activation energy, increasing the rate so equilibrium is reached faster at a lower temperature, saving energy costs. It does not change the equilibrium yield.

questions.question: The formulae of two isomers, compound J (methyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) and compound K (2-methylpropanoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$), are shown. Identify the type of isomer shown.
questions.answer: Functional group isomers (J is an ester and K is a carboxylic acid, both $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$).

questions.question: The formulae of two isomers, compound J (methyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) and compound K (2-methylpropanoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$), are shown. A student was provided with the mass spectrum, IR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum for both compounds (shown: one set of spectra on the left, one on the right). Identify which set of spectra belongs to compound J and which belongs to compound K.
questions.answer: The **left** spectra belong to **compound K** (2-methylpropanoic acid) and the **right** spectra belong to **compound J** (methyl propanoate).

questions.question: The formulae of two isomers, compound J (methyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) and compound K (2-methylpropanoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$), are shown. A student was provided with the mass spectrum, IR spectrum and $^{13}$C NMR spectrum for both compounds (shown: one set on the left, one on the right). The left set belongs to K and the right set to J. Explain this reasoning, referencing all the spectral data.
questions.answer:
**Infrared spectra.** Both spectra show a strong, sharp C=O absorption near 1700–1750 cm$^{-1}$ and C–H absorptions near 2850–3000 cm$^{-1}$, as both compounds contain a carbonyl group. The left spectrum also has a very broad absorption from about 2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$, characteristic of the O–H of a carboxylic acid, so it belongs to K. The right spectrum has no broad O–H band (only the narrow C–H peaks near 3000 cm$^{-1}$) but shows a strong C–O stretch near 1200 cm$^{-1}$, consistent with the ester J.

**Mass spectra.** Both show a molecular ion at m/z = 88, as both are $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ (isomers). Left spectrum: base peak at 43 = $[\text{CH(CH}_3)_2]^+$ (isopropyl cation, from loss of COOH), 73 = $[\text{M} - \text{CH}_3]^+$ = $[\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{COOH}]^+$, and 27 = $[\text{C}_2\text{H}_3]^+$. These fit the branched acid K. Right spectrum: base peak at 57 = $[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}]^+$ (propanoyl cation, from loss of $\text{OCH}_3$), 29 = $[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2]^+$ and 15 = $[\text{CH}_3]^+$. These fit the ester J.

**$^{13}$C NMR spectra.** K has 3 carbon environments (the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are equivalent by symmetry): the left spectrum has 3 peaks, at about 184 ppm (C=O of the acid), 34 ppm (CH) and 19 ppm (the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$, tallest peak). J has 4 carbon environments: the right spectrum has 4 peaks, at about 174 ppm (ester C=O), 51 ppm ($\text{CH}_3$ bonded to O, shifted downfield by the electronegative oxygen), 27 ppm ($\text{CH}_2$) and 9 ppm ($\text{CH}_3$).

All three techniques therefore consistently show that the left spectra are K and the right spectra are J.

questions.question:
Some thermochemical data relating to potassium hydroxide is shown below.

$$\text{KOH}(s) \rightarrow \text{K}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \qquad \Delta H = -57.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
$$\text{KOH}(s) + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \qquad \Delta H = -59.1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

An 80.0 mL sample of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ was poured into a polystyrene foam cup. A temperature probe placed into the acid recorded an initial temperature of 24.3 °C. 5.00 g of KOH was then added to the acid and completely dissolved in it. The probe was used to determine the highest temperature reached upon this dissolution.

Show by calculation which is the limiting reagent in the reaction between potassium hydroxide and sulfuric acid.
questions.answer:
$2\text{KOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$

$n(\text{KOH}) = \dfrac{5.00}{39.10 + 16.00 + 1.008} = \dfrac{5.00}{56.108} = 0.0891$ mol

$n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4) = 0.50 \times 0.0800 = 0.040$ mol

The 2 : 1 ratio means 0.040 mol $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ needs $2 \times 0.040 = 0.080$ mol KOH. Since $0.0891 > 0.080$, KOH is in excess and **$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is the limiting reagent**.

questions.question:
Some thermochemical data relating to potassium hydroxide is shown below.

$$\text{KOH}(s) \rightarrow \text{K}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \qquad \Delta H = -57.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
$$\text{KOH}(s) + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \qquad \Delta H = -59.1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

An 80.0 mL sample of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ was poured into a polystyrene foam cup. A temperature probe placed into the acid recorded an initial temperature of 24.3 °C. 5.00 g of KOH was then added to the acid and completely dissolved in it. The probe was used to determine the highest temperature reached upon this dissolution.

In this mixture $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (0.040 mol) is the limiting reagent and KOH (0.0891 mol) is in excess. Calculate the highest theoretical temperature which could be measured by the probe, assuming no energy loss to the environment.
questions.answer:
0.080 mol of solid KOH reacts with the acid (second equation, which starts from KOH(s), so it already includes dissolving that KOH):
$q_1 = 0.080 \times 59.1 = 4.728$ kJ

The excess KOH, $0.0891 - 0.080 = 0.0091$ mol, only dissolves (first equation):
$q_2 = 0.00911 \times 57.6 = 0.525$ kJ

Total heat released $q = 4.728 + 0.525 = 5.253$ kJ $= 5253$ J

Assuming the solution has the mass (80.0 g, density 1 g mL$^{-1}$) and specific heat capacity of water:
$$\Delta T = \frac{q}{mc} = \frac{5253}{80.0 \times 4.18} = 15.7\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

Highest temperature $= 24.3 + 15.7 = 40.0$ °C.

*Note: the school's answer (53.8 °C) adds the dissolution enthalpy for all 0.0891 mol of KOH to the second equation's enthalpy for 0.080 mol, double-counting the dissolution of the 0.080 mol that reacts (the second equation already starts from solid KOH). It would only be right if −59.1 kJ mol$^{-1}$ were the neutralisation of already-dissolved KOH.*

questions.question:
Evaluate the following statement. Refer to the provided data and use appropriate chemical equations.

*"Biofuels are a better option than traditional fossil fuels as an energy source."*

| Fuel | Formula | $\Delta H^\circ_c$ (kJ/g) |
|---|---|---|
| Octane (petrol) | $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}$ | 48 |
| Diesel | $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{26}$ | 44 |
| Biodiesel | $\text{C}_{11}\text{H}_{26}\text{O}_2$ – $\text{C}_{19}\text{H}_{34}\text{O}_2$ | 40 – 48* |
| Ethanol | $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ | 29.78 |

*Biodiesel can have varying chain lengths.
questions.answer:
**Biofuels** are made from renewable biological sources. Ethanol is produced by fermentation of glucose from crops such as sugarcane or corn (yeast, about 37 °C, anaerobic):
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq) + 2\text{CO}_2(g)$$
Biodiesel is made from vegetable oils or animal fats (transesterification with methanol).

**Energy content.** Biodiesel releases 40–48 kJ/g, comparable to diesel (44 kJ/g) and octane (48 kJ/g), so it is an effective direct replacement. Ethanol releases only 29.78 kJ/g, about 60% of octane, so more fuel (and larger tanks/more frequent refuelling) is needed for the same energy; however, it is miscible with petrol and can be blended (e.g. E10) to reduce fossil fuel use.

**Combustion equations.**
- Ethanol: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(l) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
- Biodiesel (e.g.): $2\text{C}_{11}\text{H}_{26}\text{O}_2(l) + 33\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 22\text{CO}_2(g) + 26\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
- Octane: $2\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}(l) + 25\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 16\text{CO}_2(g) + 18\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
- Diesel: $2\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{26}(l) + 37\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 24\text{CO}_2(g) + 26\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

Biofuels contain oxygen in their molecules, which promotes complete combustion. Long-chain fossil fuels are more likely to undergo incomplete combustion, e.g. $2\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18} + 24\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 14\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{CO} + 2\text{C} + 18\text{H}_2\text{O}$, producing toxic CO and soot (particulates). Fossil fuels can also contain sulfur impurities, producing $\text{SO}_2$ and acid rain.

**Carbon cycle.** The $\text{CO}_2$ released when biofuels burn was recently absorbed by plants in photosynthesis, $6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$, so biofuels are potentially close to carbon neutral. Fossil fuels release carbon that was sequestered for millions of years, increasing atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$ and contributing to climate change and ocean acidification. Fossil fuels are also non-renewable and will run out.

**Limitations of biofuels.** Growing, harvesting, fermenting and distilling require energy (often from fossil fuels), so they are not fully carbon neutral; large areas of farmland are needed, competing with food production and causing land clearing; and engines/infrastructure may need modification.

**Judgement:** Overall, biofuels are a better option than fossil fuels as an energy source, because they are renewable, burn more cleanly and have a much smaller net impact on atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$, while biodiesel matches fossil fuels in energy content. Their lower energy density (ethanol) and land-use issues mean they are best used alongside, and progressively replacing, fossil fuels.

*Note: the school's sample answer gives an unbalanced biodiesel equation ($17\text{O}_2$; it should be $33\text{O}_2$ for $2\text{C}_{11}\text{H}_{26}\text{O}_2$) and unbalanced ethanol combustion and fermentation equations; balanced versions are given above.*
